Adding an expense · the canvas

Every page of the design canvas for this exploration, flattened into one file on 2026-10-06. The live canvas is at claude.ai/artifact/A8CUNvsPrYMjek5S2a64Rm. Pages run in the order they were made.

1 · Directions

Adding an expense · four directions

TODAY. After €12 the keypad stays up and has no key that moves on. The name is a faint line you have to find and tap. Date and repeat already hold today and monthly, but their buttons look just like the empty category button, so it reads as five questions where three are needed. Netflix, with categories made: digits, tap the name, type, tap the category button, tap Streaming, ✓. Four taps plus typing, and nothing says which comes next. First bill: category button, New category, an emoji, a name, a colour, then ✓. About seven taps, and a filing system designed before the first bill is saved.
A · ONE SCREEN THAT LEADS. Recommended. The keypad gets a Next key, so the amount hands on to the name. While you type the name, your categories ride above the keyboard, most recent first, with the likely one outlined (page 2). Date and repeat become one quiet line, 'today · every month', that reads as settled and opens the same pickers when tapped. Netflix: digits, Next, name, chip, ✓. Three taps. Serves tenet 2 (the amount stays the screen, the next thing is always obvious) and 3 (the defaults read as done, without labels). Strains little; it is still a form, so the breeze has to come from the chips. Leans on TASTE 11: a bar above the keyboard is where iOS already offers suggestions. Editing opens as A3 does, filled in.
B · SET ASIDE: too constricted; no steppers. B · ONE THING AT A TIME. Each step is its own screen. Answers collapse into a line at the top that you tap to go back. The defaults are asked once, together, as a sentence you accept with ✓. Netflix: digits, Next, name, Next, chip, ✓. Four taps, but never a doubt about what comes next. Serves tenet 1 for a newcomer. Strains TASTE 12 (a sequence must stay jumpable, and the dots have to be real buttons) and editing, which has to show everything at once, so the two screens diverge. It's the walkthrough that lost in round 1, on paper; drawn again because the complaint now comes from the hand.
C · SET ASIDE: too close to the editor as it is. C · NAME FIRST. You say what it is before how much. The name is where a guess comes from, so by the time the keypad is up the category is already filled in, outlined as the app's guess (C2). A wrong guess is one tap to the list (C3). Netflix: type, Next, digits, ✓. Two taps. Thinks ahead the most. Strains DESIGN's 'the amount is the screen': the amount opens second and the screen opens on a keyboard. Hinges on page 2's rule that ✓ takes an outlined guess.
D · TAKEN FURTHER on page 0. D · THE BILL AS A SENTENCE. Under the amount, one sentence: 'for Netflix, every month from today, in 📺 Streaming'. The defaults are words that already read as done; what's missing is the only blue. Tap any word and its picker opens where the keypad was, as today. Netflix: digits, Next, name, tap the guess, ✓. Three taps. A fourth direction because it answers 'the defaults look unfinished' with language rather than layout. Strains tenet 3: 'for', 'every' and 'in' are words doing label work. It is also the hardest at accessibility sizes, where a sentence wraps into a paragraph.

2 · Later bills

Later bills · the app thinks ahead

Three ways to think ahead once categories exist. They stack: T1 is the floor, T2 and T3 add to it, and each works in any direction on page 1. T1 · Recent first. The chips live in the sheet rather than on the keyboard, so they survive the keyboard closing. They are ordered by last used and scroll sideways. Needs no model. T2 · A guess, outlined. The category button fills itself from the name, outlined with a spark until you take it. Matching past names needs no model; Foundation Models would guess for a name never seen before ('Spotify' → 📺). Where guesses come from is a later discussion. T3 · A bill you've had before. Typing a name you've used offers the whole bill back: amount, category, repeat. Useful for a bill that ended and restarts, or a second gym. Open question for all three: does ✓ take an outlined guess, or must you tap it first? Taking it saves a tap. Requiring it means nothing is ever filed where you didn't look.

3 · First bill

First bill · no categories yet

The heaviest moment, and the one that decides whether tenet 4 is rewritten. F1 · Made where the chips will go. Emoji, then name, in the row that later holds your categories, without leaving the screen. The colour is picked for you. Keeps tenet 4 as written. Still asks you to design a category, just in fewer places. F2 · The app proposes the first. From the name, one tap makes '📺 Streaming'. Rename or recolour later in Settings. Strains tenet 4: a suggested category is a small starter set, unless it's only ever built from what you typed. F3 · Save now, file later. Amount and name are enough. The bill lands on the timeline with an empty grey well, and in the category view in a lane with no emoji. Rewrites tenet 4 and 'Every expense has a category'. Something then has to invite filing it without becoming a chore (tenet 1), and that is unsolved here.

0 · D in depth

D in depth · the bill as a sentence

THE FLOW. You never have to tap the underlined words. Next walks only the blanks: amount → name → category, then ✓. The underlined words are defaults you can leave alone. Tap one only to change it, and its picker opens where the keypad was (row 2). Netflix, with categories: digits, Next, type the name, next, tap 📺, ✓. Three taps, or two if ✓ takes the guess. The category picker is your categories as chips, recent first, the guess outlined, New last. The date now reads 'Sep 30' rather than 'today' (see A′ below).
PROS AND CONS OF THE SENTENCE For • Defaults read as done: they're words, not empty-looking buttons. • What's missing is the only blue, so the next step shows without a stepper. • It reads back what you'll get. 'every 3 months from Sep 30, 4 times' is a check three icons can't give. • Words carry states icons can't: 'starting' for a date ahead, 'on' for one charge. Against • Tenet 3: 'for', 'every' and 'in' are small labels. • It reflows as values change. 'every 3 months' pushes the category onto a new line, so words move under your eye (TASTE 2). • Inline words are small targets. The line height has to give each one 44pt. • Accessibility sizes turn it into a paragraph (S8). • Building it: SwiftUI can make words inside wrapped text tappable, for free. A text field inside a sentence (S2) isn't stock; S10 avoids it. • Word order is English. Another language needs its own sentence.
CHANGING A DEFAULT, AND EDITING S5 · Every 3 months with an end, both said back in words. 'Last payment Jun 30, 2027' stays under the wheel. S6 · A date ahead reads 'starting Mar 14' rather than 'from'. The word does what the calendar-with-a-clock icon does today. S7 · Opening an existing charge. Its date belongs to this charge, not to the bill's start, so the sentence says 'on Oct 30'; 'from' would be wrong. Trash stays left of ✓.
THE HARD CASES S8 · An accessibility text size. The sentence wraps to six lines but still reads. Open: keep it as a sentence at these sizes, or stack it into rows, as the three buttons stack today? S9 · Dark. S10 · A lighter D. The name keeps its own line, a plain text field as today, and the sentence carries only what you pick. It drops 'for' and the hardest part to build, typing inside a sentence.
A′ · YOUR TWO QUESTIONS ABOUT A The date, not 'today'. 'Sep 30 · every month'. A date is always true; 'today' stops being true tomorrow, when you open the bill again. It also matches the timeline rows. Categories in the sheet, not on the keyboard. On the keyboard they'd sit on top of iOS's own suggestion bar and vanish when the keyboard closes. In the sheet they stay put while you move between keypad, keyboard and pickers.

R3 · The card

Round 3 · A card you complete

HOW TO READ THIS PAGE One row per hierarchy, four moments each: empty, half done, complete, and a first bill with no categories. Only the information order differs between rows. Look, type and colour are placeholders for the design pass. The same rules hold in every row: • Dashed means it still needs you. Blue dashed is the one the card is pulling you to next. • Date and repeat arrive filled in, as Oct 4 and Monthly, because the app has already chosen them. • ✓ top right is the only button. Nothing below the card says Next. You move on by tapping the card's next dashed part, or with the keyboard's return key. • Whatever you tap opens its picker where the keys are, as today.
A · AMOUNT, THEN THREE ROWS. Your sketch. Recommended. The amount leads. Under it, three equal rows: the category's emoji beside the name, then the date, then the repeat. Every row is a full-width target and opens its own picker. iCloud, with categories made: digits, tap the name, type, then ✓, which takes the guessed category. Two taps plus typing. Serves tenet 2 and tenet 3: icons label the rows without words. It also fixes the accessibility problem, because the rows are already stacked. Editing a charge can use the same card, filled in. Strains: it is still a list of fields. The dashes are what stop it from reading as a form. Leans on TASTE 5, a mark only where it distinguishes. Compare A0 on the right: with all four dashed, dashes stop meaning "missing" and the card reads as four questions where two are left.
B · YOUR PART ABOVE, THE APP'S BELOW The amount, then the name and emoji, larger. Date and repeat drop to a quiet footer line on the card's bottom edge. The split follows who supplies each value. You supply the amount, name and category, so they get the face. The app supplies the date and repeat, so they recede. Serves the brief's third goal most, defaults that read as done. Strains: the date and repeat become smaller targets, and a yearly bill or a later start, the cases that need changing, sit in the smallest type. At accessibility sizes the footer wraps.
C · A STAMP AND A STUB The category leaves the rows and becomes a stamp in the card's corner. Date and repeat sit on a stub along the bottom, two equal halves like today's buttons. This is the bridge to filing. Today you tap the stamp. Later, dragging the card into a pocket fills the stamp, so the card never has to change shape for that. Serves the follow-on work, and gives a first bill an obvious empty corner. Strains: the emoji is no longer beside the name, so the card stops previewing the timeline row. A ticket shape is also partly a matter of style, and style is meant to come later.
IN THE PROTOTYPE: A AND C https://claude.ai/artifact/BH2CKwEpj7w3E7BfJawSWa (docs/prototypes/edit-revisit-card.html). There you can switch between them mid-entry. It adds what still images can't show: the name's dashes turning blue once the amount is in, the guess appearing as you type, the keys changing under the card, and a first bill that makes its category in place.

R4 · Playful cards

Round 4 · Playful cards

FIVE WAYS TO MAKE IT FUN Each row is one idea about what the card is, drawn at its key moments. The look is a sketch of the idea and isn't a proposal for the visual design. What stays the same in every row: ✓ top right is the only button. The date is real. The category is guessed from the name. Whatever you tap opens where the keys are. Nothing below the card says Next. The test for each one: the fun has to come from something true about bills, or it's decoration (tenet 2). And no moment may hold up the next tap (TASTE 12).
S · STAMPS AND A POSTMARK Your categories are rubber stamps, each with its name inked round the ring. Tap one and it thunks onto the card at a slight angle, with a haptic. The guess is already lifted out of the tray. The date and repeat are a postmark the app has already inked, so they read as done without any dashes. First bill: you make a stamp. Pick an emoji and it sits in the middle; as you type the category's name, it curls round the ring (S4). Making a category becomes the fun part, not the chore. Serves the first-bill problem best. Strains: the amount and the stamp compete for attention, and with twenty categories the tray needs to scroll. Cost: text on a circle isn't stock in SwiftUI. It's a small custom view, drawn letter by letter. Bridge to folders: the stamp is the category, so filing could become stamping.
L · THE CARD THAT SHOWS WHAT'S COMING. Recommended. An index card, with the next charges stamped down its ruled lines: Oct 4 inked, and Nov, Dec and Jan faint behind it. Change the repeat to every 3 months and the faint stamps re-ink as Jan, Apr, Jul (L2). The category is a tab on the card's top edge. The delight here is information. You see what the bill will do before you save it, which is Tilly's whole job (job 1, forward visibility). Leans on TASTE 7: the figure sits on the thing it describes. Strains: the most "card-like" of the five, and the least silly. The ruled lines are a skin the design pass might drop. Cost: low. It's text and rotation, all stock. Bridge to folders: a tabbed card is literally what goes in a folder. The tab is what you'd hold it by.
K · STICKERS Categories are stickers on a sheet where the keys were, with a white die-cut edge like iOS's own stickers. The guess is already peeled and lifted (K2). Drag it or tap it, and it slaps onto the card's corner at an angle, over the card's edge (K3). First bill: a blank die-cut outline. Pick an emoji and it gets cut into your first sticker, then you name it (K4). Serves delight with the least explaining, because everyone knows stickers. Leans on TASTE 11, iOS's own sticker look. Strains: dragging is a second way to do what a tap does. Cost: drag and drop is stock. The white edge is a stock shadow trick. Bridge to folders: the strongest. If you already drag a sticker onto a card, dragging the card into a pocket is the same hand.
V · THE CARD DEVELOPS, LIKE A PHOTO The card starts grey and undeveloped. What the app filled in, the date and repeat, is already sharp. The rest develops as you add it. When the category lands, its colour spreads from the emoji (V2), and the finished card is in your category's colour (V3). This is A from round 3 with a payoff. The colour is the one you chose for the category, so finishing the card puts your colour on it. Serves the pull to finish: a half-grey card wants to be finished. Strains: grey can read as disabled. In dark mode, white text on a light category colour needs care. Cost: low. It's a colour animation. Bridge to folders: neutral.
T · A TRADING CARD. The wild one. Each bill is a collectible card: name and cost along the top, an art window in the category's colour with its emoji, a type line, "Monthly · Storage", a line of flavour text, and a collector number. This is your eighth card. Holo sheen when it's complete, tilting with the phone. Fun, and it gives every bill a face. Strains tenet 2 hard: the art is the biggest thing and the amount moves to a corner. The flavour text is pure decoration, and it would need writing. Cost: the highest. Generated art per bill, plus motion sensing for the sheen. Drawn so the boundary is visible: this is how far "fun" can go before it costs the hierarchy.
SMALL DELIGHTS THAT FIT ANY ROW • Digits roll as you type, like an odometer. SwiftUI does this for free (numeric text transition). • ✓ lands with a soft thunk, a haptic, and the card dips before it leaves. • The finished card tilts slightly with the phone, catching light the way Wallet's cards do. • The date drawn as a little Calendar app icon: weekday on top, the day big beneath. • The guess arrives with a small wiggle, once, never looping.
WHERE THESE CAME FROM (from memory, not checked live) • Arc's membership card: stamps earned per anniversary (yours). → S • Flighty: boarding-pass cards, and a passport of stamps for places you've flown. → S, L • Apple Wallet: a card slides into the stack; tickets tear along perforations; sheen when you tilt. → filing, T • Things 3's Magic Plus: drag + to where the item belongs. → filing • iMessage and iOS stickers: peel and slap, white die-cut edge. → K • Monzo Pots: money in named pockets, each with a picture. → folders • Lapse and Retro: photos that develop later. → V • Pokémon TCG Pocket: opening packs, holo shimmer. → T • Partiful and Luma: invites as playful, themed cards. Most of this is motion, so screen recordings would help more than screenshots. Mobbin's flow videos for these apps are a good start.

R5 · Ten cards

Round 5 · Ten cards

TEN CARDS, EACH WITH A LOOK AND A BEHAVIOUR. Two frames each: the moment that makes it fun, and the card finished. Same bill throughout: iCloud, €15.99, Oct 4, monthly, guessed into ☁️ Storage. The looks are sketches of the idea. The design pass still owns them. Held in every one: ✓ top right is the only button, nothing says Next, nothing blocks the next tap. MY SHORTLIST TO PROTOTYPE: 1 Wallet, 5 Date stamper and 4 Stamps. Reasons are in each note. The trading card from round 4 is still on that page.
1 · WALLET. Recommended. (Apple Wallet) The bill is a card in its category's colour. Swipe it sideways to change category, like flicking through Wallet. The guess is the first card, and dots show there are more. The last swipe is a blank card: a new category. On ✓ the card drops into the stack of your other bills and the sheet closes. Choosing a category stops being a list. It's picking which card this is. The colour is the one you chose (it's yours). First bill: swiping goes through blank cards in the eight colours. Stop on one and give it an emoji. Strains: a sideways swipe is hidden without the dots. The stack looks like a second list of bills, when the timeline is the list. Cost: low. Paging is stock, and the stack is only the landing moment. Leans on TASTE 11: Wallet's own vocabulary.
2 · BOARDING PASS (Flighty, Wallet passes) A tall pass: the category as the coloured band at the top, the amount set like a flight number, the date and repeat as the pass's details. Below the tear line, a barcode prints a third at a time as the amount, name and category go in. A full barcode means ready. The barcode is a progress bar that doesn't look like one. You can see what's left without a single dashed field. Strains: the barcode is decoration that stands in for information. It encodes nothing. Tall, so it barely fits above the keyboard. Cost: low.
3 · FLIP CARD (the back of a Wallet pass) The front is only the amount, huge, the purest form of "the amount is the screen". Once it's in, the card turns over. The back has the name, your categories printed on it with the guess outlined, and the date and repeat. The amount stays as a pill in the corner; tap it to turn back. Two sides, not two steps: you can turn it whenever you like (TASTE 12). Strains: the turn is a moving primary action in disguise, so it has to be automatic. The back can drift towards a form. Cost: low. It's a stock 3D rotation.
4 · STAMPS (Arc's card, Flighty's passport) From round 4. Your categories are rubber stamps; tap one and it thunks on with a haptic. The date and repeat are a postmark the app has already inked. First bill: you make your first stamp, and the category's name curls round the ring as you type. The best answer to the first bill. Making a category becomes the fun part. Strains: the amount and the stamp compete. Twenty categories means a scrolling tray. Cost: medium. Text on a circle is custom.
5 · DATE STAMPER (a library card and a rubber date stamp) Round 4's index card, with a new behaviour. Tap the stamps and a rubber date stamper opens where the keys were: bands for month, day and repeat. Roll them, and the stamps down the card re-ink as you roll: Nov 12, Dec 12, Jan 12… The fun is information, which is Tilly's job: you see what the bill will do before you save it. Leans on TASTE 7. Strains: the least silly of the ten. The bands are a custom wheel. Cost: medium. Three wheel pickers styled as rubber.
6 · STICKERS (iOS and iMessage stickers) From round 4. Categories are die-cut stickers on a sheet; the guess is already peeled. Drag or tap, and it slaps on over the card's edge at an angle. Needs no explaining. Same hand as dragging into a folder later. Strains: a drag is a second way to do a tap. Cost: low. Drag and drop and the white edge are stock.
7 · POLAROID (Lapse, Retro) The card is a photo. You write the amount and name on its border in marker. The photo is blank until the category lands; then it develops over a couple of seconds into the category's colour and emoji, and ✓ works the whole time. Warm, personal, a little nostalgic. Strains tenet 2: the photo is the biggest thing and the amount is a caption. Handwriting at accessibility sizes. The photo is decoration: it shows the category, nothing more. Cost: medium. Only the font and the develop effect.
8 · LABEL MAKER (Dymo tape) The name punches into embossed tape a letter at a time, with a click for each. Things the app filled in, the date and repeat, are on black tape already. Choosing a category means choosing a tape cartridge, and the name's tape takes its colour. Labels are what you use for filing, so the metaphor is honest about what categories are for. Strains: capitals only, so names lose their own spelling (iCloud becomes ICLOUD). Embossed type at small sizes. Cost: low. Type and a shape.
9 · PUNCH CARD (Arc's generated art, a coffee loyalty card) Art at the top grows from the name as you type: every letter moves the shapes, so each bill gets its own picture. It takes the category's colour. Underneath, a punch for each of the next twelve charges, the first one punched: a monthly bill shows twelve, a yearly one shows one. The art is a face for the bill. The punches are forward visibility again. Strains tenet 2: the art is the biggest thing, and it's decoration. A weekly bill needs 52 punches. Cost: medium to high. Generated shapes.
10 · DROP IT ON THE DAY (Things 3's Magic Plus) A behaviour more than a look. Drag + off the header and down the timeline; a line and a day show where it would land. Let go and the card opens with that date already set (the clock calendar, because it's ahead). Tapping + still opens on today. The date is chosen by place, in the list you already read. It is also the landing animation in reverse: the card leaves from the spot it will return to. Strains: dragging between rows has to pick days that hold no bill, so the line needs a day readout. Hidden unless you know. Cost: medium. A drag gesture over the list.

R6 · Five more, physical

Round 6 · Five more, physical

WHAT CHANGED FROM ROUND 5. Most of those ten were skins: a metaphor painted over the same five fields. Here each field becomes something you handle, and each card is built around one feeling. Two rules, from Apple's and Emil Kowalski's design guidance: • Delight is allowed here because adding a bill is rare. You do it a few times a year, and a rare action can carry a moment that a daily one can't. • The physics has to tell the truth. A deck that's twelve cards deep is twelve charges, and a light that comes on means it's filed. Fun that isn't also information is decoration (tenet 2). Held in all five: ✓ top right is the only button, nothing says Next, the date is real, the category is guessed, and every motion can be interrupted.
1 · THE DECK. Feeling: understanding. Recommended. The repeat is the card's thickness. A monthly bill sits on a deck of eleven more, one for every charge in the next year; a yearly bill is a single card. Under the deck, what that adds up to: "12 a year · €192". Pull the deck down and it deals out into the year, each card carrying its date, with a tick as each one lands. Push it back up to stack it. Change the repeat and the deck grows or thins in front of you. Better than round 5's date stamper: the same truth, but it's the card itself rather than stamps printed on it, and the yearly total turns up without being asked for. Leans on TASTE 7, the figure on the thing it describes, and on Apple's "a small input, a big output". Strains: weekly is 52 cards. It needs a rule, such as a thicker edge rather than more cards. Cost: medium. A drag with momentum and a stack of views.
2 · IT ASSEMBLES ITSELF. Feeling: effortless, "it knows me". After the amount, you type the name, and the card fills itself in around you. The guessed emoji flies in and lands in its slot, the category's colour washes in from the corner, and the date and repeat settle into place one after another. You watch the app do the work. What's wrong, you flick off. The piece spins away, its slot goes back to dashed, and that part asks again (A2). A name you've used before brings its amount too, marked as the app's (A3). The cause is always visible: you typed, and it answered (TASTE 4). Strains: it's only as good as the guess. The flick-off is a gesture people have to discover, so a tap on the piece does the same. Cost: low for the motion; the guessing is a separate question.
3 · SPLIT-FLAP BOARD (an airport departures board). Feeling: anticipation, a little theatre. The card is a departures board. Every keystroke clatters into its tile. The category tile flips through your categories, one per tap, with the guess first; hold it for the full list. A status tile in amber says when it next goes out: TODAY, or IN 12 DAYS. The sound and the clatter make typing a name feel like an event, and the status tile is real information. Strains: capitals only. Tile width caps how long a name can be (a long one scrolls). Reduced motion swaps the flips for a fade. Cost: medium-high. A custom flip on every tile.
4 · A HAND OF CARDS (Balatro, every card game). Feeling: play. The bill is a playing card: its amount in the corners like a rank, the category as its suit. Your categories are the hand fanned where the keys were, with the guess raised. Tap one, or drag it up, and it flies onto the bill and becomes the suit in both corners. A first bill has one blank card in the hand: you draw your first suit (emoji, name, colour). Cards under your finger tilt toward it and spring back, the "juice" Balatro is loved for. Categories as suits is a mapping people already understand. Strains: twenty categories won't fan; past seven it needs to scroll. The date and repeat are small. Cost: medium. The fan and the tilt are custom; the drag is stock.
5 · POCKET DEVICE (Teenage Engineering's gadgets). Feeling: tactile joy. The card is a little gadget. An LCD shows the amount and name. A knob sets how often, with a detent tick at each stop: W, 2W, M, 3M, Y. A thumbwheel rolls the date. Your categories are keys with their colour on the cap; press one, it sinks, and its light comes on. The keypad becomes chunky keys, with an orange delete. Every control is something you'd want to touch, and there isn't a field in sight. Strains: TASTE 11, nothing here is stock. Two keyboards (the keypad and the system one for the name) clash in style. Knob labels W and 2W are terse. Cost: high. All custom controls, plus haptics on every detent.

R7 · What can I change?

Round 7 · What can I change?

YOUR NOTE: nothing says which parts of the card you can change. One rule for every row: dashed means it still needs you; a mark means it's filled in and you can change it. Marks go on the date, the repeat, and the category once it's set, never on a dashed part. The amount and name don't get one; tapping them shows a caret. All four are also a switch in the prototype, so you can feel them. Every tappable part now also dips slightly when pressed, so a touch confirms it's a control.
NONE. As it is today. The card reads cleanly, but a filled-in date looks finished rather than changeable. This is the problem you named.
PENCIL. Recommended, your idea. A small grey pencil after each value, and a badge on things that aren't text: the emoji, the stamp, the postmark, the inked date. It says "edit" in a word everyone knows. It also completes a grammar with the dashes: dashed means it needs you, a pencil means it's filled in and yours to change, and the spark means it's the app's guess (TASTE 5, every mark distinguishes something). Cost: none. One glyph. Watch for: on a card with four of them, pencils can start to look like a form's edit buttons. Keep them small and grey.
CHEVRON. iOS's own sign for "tap for choices", the up-and-down arrows on every menu and pop-up button (TASTE 11). It's the most precise of the four: the date, repeat and category are all choices from a list or calendar, which is exactly what this glyph promises. Less friendly than a pencil, and on the stamps and inked date the badge reads oddly.
PILL. The value sits in a grey capsule, like iOS's compact date picker. The most native-looking, and the strongest signal of all four. But it turns every value back into a button, and the card starts to look like the form we're trying to leave. On the Wallet it's the clearest of the four, since a white pill on colour reads as a control.

Parts

Shared parts, imported by every artboard. Keypad takes 'next' (a label for a tall key on the right). Keyboard takes 'chips' (kinds sug, on, new, plain), 'ret' and 'go'.
